name: Surgical Hemorrhagic Shock and Massive Transfusion Protocols

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / ATLS 10th ed
clinicalPearls: ATLS Shock classification: Class I (<15% loss, normal vitals), Class II (15-30%, tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure), Class III (30-40%, hypotension), Class IV (>40%, lethargic/comatose)
Trauma lethal triad: hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis; damage control resuscitation aims to prevent this downward spiral
Damage control resuscitation utilizes 1:1:1 balanced transfusion of packed RBCs, fresh frozen plasma and platelets, avoiding large-volume crystalloids
Permissive hypotension targets systolic BP 80-90 mmHg until surgical hemostasis is achieved, preventing clot blow-off
Massive transfusion protocol complications: hypocalcemia (citrate binding), hyperkalemia (lysed stored red cells), hypothermia, TRALI
reference.pathophysiology: Severe hemorrhagic shock causes systemic microvascular hypoperfusion, tissue hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism with lactic acidosis. Uncontrolled bleeding triggers trauma-induced coagulopathy (TIC) driven by endothelial glycocalyx degradation, hyperfibrinolysis and consumption of coagulation factors. Large-volume isotonic crystalloids worsen hypothermia and dilute clotting factors.
additionalInvestigations: Serial venous/arterial blood gas and lactate clearance monitoring
Rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) or Thromboelastography (TEG) for targeted blood component therapy
Ionized calcium and potassium monitoring every 4 units of PRBCs
